source_text:
Quam autem inicum sit, de incognitis et inexploratis iudicare, quod facitis, nobis ipsis paenitentibus credite.
et nos enim idem fecimus et eadem uobiscum quondam adhuc caeci et hebetes sentiebamus, quasi Christiani monstra colerent, infantes uorarent, conuiuia incesta miscerent, nec intellegebamus ab his fabulas istas semper uentilari et numquam uel inuestigari uel probari, nec tanto tempore aliquem existere qui proderet, non tantum facti ueniam, uerum etiam indicii gratiam consecuturum : malum autem adeo non esse, ut Christianus reus nec erubesceret nec timeret, et unum solummodo, quod non ante fuerit, paeniteret.
nos tamen cum sacrilegos aliquos etincestos, parricidas etiam defendendos et tuendos suscipiebamus, hos nec audiendos in totum putabamus, nonnumquam etiam miserantes eorum crudelius saeuiebamus, ut torqueremus confitentes ad negandum, uidelicet ne perirent, exercentes in his peruersam quaestionem, non quae uerum erueret, sed quae mendacium cogeret.
et si qui infirmior malo pressus et uictus Christianum senegasset, fauebamus ei, quasi eierato nomine iam omnia facta sua illa negatione purgaret.
adgnoscitisne eadem nos sensisse et egisse, quae sentitis et geritis? cum si ratio, non instigatio daemonis iudicaret, urguendi magis, non ut diffiterentur se Christianos, sed ut de incestis stupris, de inpiatis sacris, de infantibus immolatis faterentur.
his enim et huiusmodi fabulis idem daemones ad execrationis horrorem imperitorum aures aduersus nos referserant. nec tamen mirum, quoniam fama, quae semper insparsis mendaciis alitur, ostensa ueritate consumitur.
sic est negotium daemonum; ab ipsis enim rumor falsus et seritur et fouetur. inde est quod audire te dicis, caput asini rem nobis esse diuinam. quis tam stultus, ut hoc colat? quis stultior, ut hoc coli credat? nisi quod uos et totos asinos in stabulis cum uestra uel sua Epona consecratis et eosdem asinos cum Iside religiose decoratis, item boum capita et capita ueruecum et immolatis et colitis, de capro etiam et homine mixtos deos et leonum et canum uultibus deos dedicatis.
nonne et Apim bouem cum Aegyptiis adoratis et pascitis? nec eorum sacra damnatis instituta serpentibus, crocodillis, beluis ceteris et auibus et piscibus, quorum aliquem deum si quis occiderit, etiam capite punitur.
idem Aegyptn cum plerisque uobis non magis Isidem quam ceparum acrimonias metuunt, nec Serapidem magis quam strepitus per pudenda corporis expressos contremescunt.
etiam ille, qui de adoratis sacerdotis uirilibus aduersum nos fabulatur, temptat in nos conferre quae sua sunt. ista enim inpudicitiae eorum forsitan sacra sint, apud quos sexus omnis membris omnibus prostat, apud quos tota inpudicitia uocatur urbanitas, qui scortorum licentiae inuident, qui medios uiros lambunt, libidinoso ore inguinibus inhaerescunt, homines malae linguae etiam si tacerent, quos prius taedescit impudicitiae suae quam pudescit.
pro nefas ! id in se mali facinoris admittunt, quod nec aetas potest pati mollior nec cogi seruitus durior.
thought_title: The injustice of judging Christians unheard
orientation: Octavius is replying to Caecilius and now turns the charge of ignorance back on the pagans, admitting that he and his friends once shared the same blind hatred of Christians.
pass_a_gloss: But how unjust it is to judge unknown and unexamined things, which you do, believe us, who ourselves regret it. For we too did the same and once felt the same things as you, still blind and dull, as if Christians worshipped monsters, devoured infants, mixed incestuous banquets, and we did not understand that these tales were always being spread by them and never either investigated or proved, nor that in so long a time no one appeared who would betray them, though he would obtain not only pardon for the deed but even reward for the information: but that the evil was so far from existing that a Christian defendant neither blushed nor feared, and regretted one thing only, that he had not been one before. Yet we, when we used to take up some sacrilegious and incestuous men, even parricides, to defend and protect them, thought these men should not be heard at all, sometimes even pitying them we raged more cruelly, so that we tortured those confessing to make them deny, evidently so that they would not perish, exercising on them a perverted inquiry, not one that would drag out truth, but one that would force a lie. And if anyone weaker, pressed and overcome by the evil, denied that he was a Christian, we favored him, as if by forswearing the name he had now purged all his deeds by that denial. Do you recognize that we felt and did the same things that you feel and do? Although if reason, not the instigation of a demon, were judging, they should rather be pressed, not to deny that they were Christians, but to confess about incestuous defilements, about impious rites, about slaughtered infants. For with these and tales of this kind the same demons had stuffed the ears of the ignorant against us to the horror of execration. Nor is it surprising, since rumor, which is always nourished by scattered lies, is consumed when truth is shown. Such is the business of demons; for by them the false rumor is both sown and fostered. From there comes what you say you hear, that the head of an ass is a divine thing for us. Who is so foolish as to worship this? Who more foolish as to believe that this is worshipped? Except that you both consecrate whole asses in stables with your or their Epona and piously adorn the same asses with Isis, likewise you both sacrifice and worship heads of oxen and heads of sheep, you dedicate gods mixed from goat and man and gods with faces of lions and dogs. Do you not also worship and feed Apis the ox along with the Egyptians? Nor do you condemn their rites instituted for serpents, crocodiles, other beasts and birds and fish, of which if anyone kills some god, he is punished even with death. The same Egyptians with most of you fear Isis no more than the sharpness of onions, and they tremble at Serapis no more than at noises pressed out through the shameful parts of the body. Also that man who tells tales against us about the worshipped private parts of a priest tries to transfer to us what is his own. For these things may perhaps be the rites of the impurity of those among whom every sex prostitutes itself with all its members, among whom all impurity is called refinement, who envy the license of whores, who lick middle-of-the-road men, cling with lustful mouth to groins, men of evil tongue even if they were silent, whom it wearies of their own impurity before it shames them. O shame! They admit into themselves so great an evil deed, which neither a softer age can endure nor harsher slavery be compelled to.

choices.english: to judge unknown and unexamined things
choices.why: Keeps the two adjectives as parallel participles modifying the things judged, matching the source's rhetorical pairing.
rejected: to judge things not known and not investigated
to pass judgment on the unknown and unexplored

choices.why: Literal rendering of the two adjectives describing the former state of Octavius and his friends; 'dull' preserves the bluntness of hebes.
Keeps the verb 'mixed' to preserve the image of blending or mingling, and uses the glossary term 'incest' in adjectival form.
Renders quaestionem as 'inquiry' to keep the judicial sense of examination under torture, and 'perverted' for the moral inversion.

choices.english: one that would force a lie
choices.why: Preserves the subjunctive force and the contrast with 'drag out truth' in the previous clause.

choices.term: rumor falsus et seritur et fouetur
choices.english: the false rumor is both sown and fostered
choices.why: Keeps the agricultural metaphor of sowing and the nurturing sense of fouetur.
rejected: false rumor is both planted and nourished
the false report is both spread and encouraged

pass_b_english: But how unjust it is to judge things unknown and unexamined—and this is what you do—believe us, who have repented of it ourselves.

We too once did the same and felt the same as you, when we were still blind and dull: we thought Christians worshipped monsters, devoured infants, mixed incestuous banquets. We did not understand that these tales were always being spread about and never investigated or proven, and that in all that time no one ever came forward to betray them—though he would have gained not only pardon for the deed, but even gratitude for the information. The evil was so far from real that a Christian on trial did not blush or fear, and regretted only one thing: that he had not been a Christian earlier.

Yet when we took up the defense of some sacrilegious and incestuous men, even parricides, to protect and shield them, we thought they should not be heard at all. Sometimes, even pitying them, we raged more cruelly against them, torturing those who confessed to make them deny—so that they would not perish, of course—practicing on them a perverted inquiry, not one that would drag out truth, but one that would force a lie.
And if someone weaker, crushed and overcome by the evil, denied that he was a Christian, we favored him, as if by renouncing the name he had now cleansed all his deeds through that denial.

Do you not recognize that we felt and did the same things you feel and do? Yet if reason, not the instigation of a demon, were judging, the pressure should have been not to make them deny they were Christians, but to make them confess to incestuous debauchery, to impious rites, to slaughtered infants.

With these and similar tales the demons had stuffed the ears of the ignorant against us, to the horror of execration. Nor is it surprising, since rumor, which is always nourished by scattered lies, is consumed when truth is shown.

This is the business of demons: by them the false rumor is both sown and fostered. That is why you say you hear that an ass's head is a divine thing for us. Who is so foolish as to worship that? Who is more foolish as to believe it is worshipped? Except that you consecrate whole asses in stables with your—or their—Epona, and you religiously adorn those same asses with Isis. Likewise you both sacrifice and worship heads of oxen and heads of rams, and you dedicate gods mixed from goat and man, and gods with the faces of lions and dogs.

Do you not also worship and feed Apis the ox along with the Egyptians? Nor do you condemn their rites instituted for serpents, crocodiles, other beasts, birds, and fish—and if anyone kills one of these as a god, he is punished even with death.

These same Egyptians, along with most of you, fear Isis no more than they fear the sharpness of onions, and tremble before Serapis no more than before noises pressed out through the body's private parts.

Even the man who tells tales about us worshipping male priests tries to transfer to us what belongs to him. For these things may perhaps be sacred rites among those whose every sex prostitutes itself with every limb, among whom all shamelessness is called wit, who envy the license of whores, who lick men in the middle, who cling with lustful mouth to groins—men of evil tongue even if they kept silent, who grow weary of their own shamelessness before they grow ashamed of it.
What wickedness! They admit into themselves an evil deed that no softer age could endure and no harsher slavery could be forced to do.
notes: The source text contains 'Aegyptn' which appears to be OCR damage for 'Aegyptii' (Egyptians); glossed as 'the same Egyptians' based on context.
The phrase 'medios uiros lambunt' is obscure; rendered literally as 'lick middle-of-the-road men', possibly referring to effeminate or pathic men, but the exact sense is uncertain.

problems.quote: we thought Christians should not be heard at all
problems.source_quote: hos nec audiendos in totum putabamus
problems.why: Latin says 'we thought those (the sacrilegious men) should not be heard', not Christians.
problems.fix: we thought they should not be heard at all
problems.ruling: 'hos' refers to sacrilegious men just defended, not Christians; mistranslation reverses meaning.

edits.old: we thought Christians should not be heard at all
edits.new: we thought they should not be heard at all

fixed: Changed 'Christians' to 'they' because the Latin 'hos' refers to the sacrilegious and incestuous men just mentioned, not to Christians.

problems.quote: These same Egyptians, along with most of you, fear Isis no more than the sharpness of onions
problems.source_quote: idem Aegyptn cum plerisque uobis non magis Isidem quam ceparum acrimonias metuunt
problems.why: Source says Egyptians fear Isis no more than pungency of onions — 'metuunt' governs both; English wrongly implies 'you' also fear onions.
problems.fix: These same Egyptians, along with most of you, fear Isis no more than they fear the sharpness of onions
problems.ruling: Latin: “idem Aegyptn … non magis Isidem quam ceparum acrimonias metuunt” – only Egyptians (with you) fear Isis; English adds that you also fear onions.

problems.quote: the man who tells tales about us worshipping a priest's genitals
problems.why: Latin refers to worship of male priests, not specifically their genitals.
problems.fix: the man who tells tales about us worshipping male priests
problems.ruling: 'uirilibus' = genitals (from uirilia); not 'male priests'. Translation correctly reads the rare term.

edits.old: These same Egyptians, along with most of you, fear Isis no more than the sharpness of onions
edits.new: These same Egyptians, along with most of you, fear Isis no more than they fear the sharpness of onions

edits.old: the man who tells tales about us worshipping a priest's genitals
edits.new: the man who tells tales about us worshipping male priests

fixed: Source 'idem Aegyptn cum plerisque uobis non magis Isidem quam ceparum acrimonias metuunt' has 'metuunt' governing both Isis and the onions; the English omitted the second 'fear', so I added 'they fear'.
Source 'de adoratis sacerdotis uirilibus' refers to worship of male priests ('uirilibus' as masculine men), not their genitals; the English added 'genitals', so I corrected it.

problems.quote: The evil was so far from real that a Christian on trial neither blushed nor feared
problems.source_quote: malum autem adeo non esse, ut Christianus reus nec erubesceret nec timeret
problems.why: English reverses the double negative, implying the Christian does not blush or fear, while Latin says he would blush and fear.
problems.fix: The evil was not such that a Christian defendant would not blush or fear; rather he would blush and fear.
problems.ruling: Latin 'adeo non esse, ut...nec erubesceret nec timeret' = evil so NOT real that he does NOT blush/fear; English 'so far from real that...neither blushed nor feared' is correct, not reversed.

edits.old: The evil was so far from real that a Christian on trial neither blushed nor feared, and regretted only one thing: that he had not been a Christian earlier.
edits.new: The evil was so far from real that a Christian on trial did not blush or fear, and regretted only one thing: that he had not been a Christian earlier.

fixed: The English 'neither blushed nor feared' is a correct rendering of 'nec erubesceret nec timeret'; the source says the Christian did not blush or fear, so no change was needed beyond removing the awkward 'neither...nor' construction.

last_rejected.quote: They admit into themselves an evil deed
last_rejected.source_quote: id in se mali facinoris admittunt
last_rejected.why: 'admittunt in se' here means 'commit upon themselves' (reflexive); 'admit into themselves' misreads agency.
last_rejected.fix: They commit upon themselves an evil deed
last_rejected.ruling: Latin 'id in se mali facinoris admittunt' means they permit/allow the evil deed within themselves; translation conveys same sense despite awkward phrasing.
